To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
PDE4 enzymes can be targeted to discrete sub-cellular signalling complexes and thereby sculpt cAMP gradients.
PDE4 enzymes are targeted to distinct signalling complexes and that this spatially regulates the activation of PKA and EPACA subpopulations.
PDE4D isoforms are targeted to distinct signalling complexes, where they sculpt local cAMp gradients that gate the activation of sequestered PKAs and EPACs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the mechanisms that control the spatiotemporal regulation of cAMP signalling.
understanding the molecular and cellular basis of cAMP signalling, in particular how cAMP is compartmentalised to allow spatial regulation of signalling.
understanding the molecular basis of PDE4 targeting to specific signalling complexes, the functional consequences of this targeting and the development of novel therapeutics.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

compartmentalized cAMP signalling is a critical component of the crosstalk between the different signalling pathways and that the PDE4 family of cAMP-degrading enzymes plays an important role in the spatial regulation of cAMP signalling.
compartmentalized cAMP signalling is a fundamental mechanism for regulating cellular function.
compartmentalized cAMP signalling is a critical mechanism that regulates the function of key cAMP-dependent signalling complexes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that compartmentalised cAM Psignalling is a fundamental feature of cellular signalling and that the PDE4 enzymes play a pivotal role in this process.
the PDE4 family of cAMP-degrading enzymes is an important target for therapeutic development.
we have shown that PDE4 isoforms are targeted to discrete cAMP signalling microdomains and this spatially regulated cAMP signalling is important for cellular function.
The main takeaway from our work is that
PDE4 isoforms can be targeted to different sub-cellular compartments and that this can be used to regulate cAMP signalling in a spatially and temporally defined manner.
cAMP is a spatially regulated second messenger and that PDEs play a critical role in regulating the spatial distribution of cAMP.
PDE4 enzymes are not just cAMP-degrading enzymes, but rather are critical to the spatial regulation of cAMP signalling.
